content: The text provided appears to be a list of references from various studies and articles related to male circumcision, particularly in the context of HIV prevention, cultural attitudes, and public health interventions. 1. Mphephu H and Timbe A, along with their colleagues, conducted a study to understand and address socio-cultural barriers to medical male circumcision in rural sub-Saharan African communities that traditionally do not practice circumcision. This research was published in Culture, Health & Sexuality in 2013. 2. Kibira SP, Makumbi F, Daniel M, Atuyambe LM, and Sandoy IF explored sexual risk behaviors and the willingness of uncircumcised adult men in Uganda to undergo circumcision. Their findings were published in PLoS One in 2015. 3. Kong X, Ssekasanvu J, Kigozi G, Lutalo T, Nalugoda F, Serwadda D, and colleagues assessed male circumcision coverage, knowledge, and attitudes after a four-year program scale-up in Rakai, Uganda. Their study appeared in AIDS Behavior in 2014. 4. Lanham M, L’Engle KL, Loolpapit M, and Oguma IO examined the roles of women in promoting voluntary medical male circumcision in Nyanza Province, Kenya. Their research was published in PLoS One in 2012. 5. Lilleston PS, Marcell AV, Nakyanjo N, Leonard L, and Wawer MJ investigated the multilevel influences on the acceptance of medical male circumcision in Rakai District, Uganda. Their findings were published in AIDS Care in 2017. 6. Lukobo MD and Bailey RC studied the acceptability of male circumcision for HIV prevention in Zambia. Their research was published in AIDS Care in 2007. 7. Macintyre K, Andrinopoulos K, Moses N, Bornstein M, Ochieng A, and Peacock E explored attitudes, perceptions, and the potential uptake of male circumcision among older men in Turkana County, Kenya, using qualitative methods. Their study was published in PLoS One in 2014. 8. MacLaren D, Tommbe R, Mafile’o T, Manineng C, Fregonese F, and Redman-MacLaren M examined beliefs and practices surrounding foreskin cutting and the acceptability of male circumcision for HIV prevention in Papua New Guinea. Their findings were published in BMC Public Health in 2013. 9. Marshall E, Rain-Taljaard R, Tsepe M, Monkwe C, Hlatswayo F, and Tshabalala S conducted sequential cross-sectional surveys in Orange Farm, South Africa, revealing consistently low uptake of voluntary medical male circumcision among adults despite demand creation campaigns. Their study appeared in PLoS One in 2016. 10. Mati K, Adegoke KK, and Salihu HM identified factors associated with married women’s support for male circumcision for HIV prevention in Uganda through a population-based cross-sectional study. Their research was published in BMC Public Health in 2016. 11. Mavhu W, Buzdugan R, Langhaug LF, Hatzold K, Benedikt C, and Sherman J investigated the prevalence and factors associated with knowledge of and willingness for male circumcision in rural Zimbabwe. Their findings were published in Tropical Medicine & International Health in 2011. 12. Miiro G, DeCelles J, Rutakumwa R, Nakiyingi-Miiro J, Muzira P, and Ssembajjwe W explored the feasibility of soccer-based promotion of voluntary medical male circumcision among secondary students in Uganda. Their study was published in PLoS One in 2017. 13. Montano DE, Kasprzyk D, Hamilton DT, Tshimanga M, and Gorn G identified key beliefs explaining adult male circumcision motivation in Zimbabwe, providing targets for behavior change messaging. Their research was published in AIDS Behavior in 2014. 14. Moyo S, Mhloyi M, Chevo T, and Rusinga O conducted a qualitative study in rural Mhondoro-Ngezi, Zimbabwe, to explore men’s attitudes as a hindrance to the demand for voluntary medical male circumcision. Their findings were published in Global Public Health in 2015. 15. Mwanza JR, Wambura M, Mosha JF, Mshana G, Mosha F, and Changalucha J analyzed the policy environment and male circumcision for HIV prevention in Tanzania through a situation analysis study. Their research was published in BMC Public Health in 2011. 16. Osaki H, Mshana G, Wambura M, Grund J, Neke N, and Kuringe E examined the role of women in promoting the uptake of voluntary medical male circumcision in Tanzania. Their study was published in PLoS One in 2015. 17. Plotkin M, Castor D, Mziray H, Kuver J, Mpuya E, and Luvanda PJ explored social and individual factors affecting adult attendance at voluntary medical male circumcision services in Tanzania. Their findings were published in Global Health Science & Practice in 2013. 18. Price JE, Phiri L, Mulenga D, Hewett PC, Topp SM, and Shiliya N conducted narrative interviews with circumcision clients in Zambia to understand behavior change pathways to voluntary medical male circumcision. Their study was published in PLoS One in 2014. 19. Rennie S, Perry B, Corneli A, Chilungo A, and Umar E examined perceptions of voluntary medical male circumcision among circumcising and non-circumcising communities in Malawi. Their findings were published in Global Public Health in 2015. 20. Rupfutse M, Tshuma C, Tshimanga M, Gombe N, Bangure D, and Wellington M identified factors associated with the uptake of voluntary medical male circumcision in Mazowe District, Zimbabwe, in 2014. Their research was published in Pan African Medical Journal in 2014.
